title: George Washington’s error
content:
In his farewell address, he said, “Our detached and distant situation invites and enables us to pursue a different course.”

It’s easy to fall in love with the idea that we live in a detached and distant situation. To imagine that culture and society and events out there have no impact on the lives we live.

The coal plant across the country, the goings on in the CEO’s office, the impact of tech on our culture… none of them are very far away. We have more leverage and connection than we want to admit.

Insulation is scarce. Technology, the competition and the shifts in media come for us, whether we seek them out or not.

It doesn’t pay to fret about things we can’t influence, but we might be able to influence more than we realize.

Perhaps isolation was useful for George. It’s clearly not true now.

[The Knowledge Project Podcast](https://fs.blog/knowledge-project-podcast/)

Elon Musk believes speed creates a competitive advantage, whether it’s speed of decision, speed of cash, or speed of response. But what does that look like day to day, and how do you build a company around it?

We also get into the five-step algorithm Jon uses to simplify problems, why Elon treats a company like a garden full of weeds, and how Tesla grew with zero marketing budget.

title: How Your Body Clock Affects Your Mental Health and Ways to Keep It in Sync
content:
Ever wondered why a bad night’s sleep can leave you irritable, anxious or sad? Poor sleep affects our emotions, but its timing also plays a role.

Our [circadian rhythms](https://theconversation.com/topics/circadian-rhythms-94) are nearly 24-hour cycles that regulate alertness, hormones, body temperature and digestion.

Deep inside the brain, a cluster of nerve cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) acts as the body’s master clock. It uses light signals from the eyes to coordinate clocks in other organs, including the brain, liver, heart and gut.

When daily routines fall out of sync with this clock, mood can suffer. Research suggests circadian disruption may contribute to mental health challenges.

Our internal clock helps regulate hormones, including melatonin and cortisol. Melatonin helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle. Levels stay low during the day, rise in the evening as darkness falls (signalling to the brain that it is time to rest), peak in the middle of the night, and drop off in the morning. Cortisol, which helps us respond to stress, typically rises towards morning.

These changes prepare the body for activity and rest, while influencing emotional wellbeing.

In a [2024 laboratory study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37648646/), my colleagues and I investigated whether our internal clocks influence mood independently of everyday activities.

We studied 19 healthy adults over 32 hours, measuring mood while minimising changes in their surroundings and behaviour.

We found that anxiety-like and depression-like mood were highest at around 8am to 9am, while participants reported greater mental fatigue and lower physical comfort between approximately 6am and 8am. These patterns were linked to their internal biological clocks, suggesting that mood can fluctuate according to biological time, independently of everyday routines.

Circadian disruption has also been [linked to depression](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38394243/) and bipolar disorder, a condition involving episodes of depression and elevated or irritable mood.

The relationship also works in both directions. Mental health difficulties can disrupt sleep and circadian rhythms, potentially creating a cycle in which low quality sleep and psychological distress reinforce one another.

**What Happens When Our Clocks Fall Out of Synch**

Night shift workers may need to stay awake when their bodies are preparing for sleep and rest when their internal clocks promote alertness.

This mismatch is known as circadian misalignment.

In a [2020 study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33122670/), we investigated how this misalignment affected mood in two controlled laboratory experiments involving people with and without shift-work experience.

Participants followed schedules designed to simulate day and night shifts while all other behavioural and environmental factors were controlled for, including light exposure, physical activity, food intake and opportunities for sleep.

We found that mood and wellbeing reduced when participants’ sleeping and waking schedules were misaligned with their internal body clock. The effects were observed in non-shift workers as well as shift workers.

These findings suggest circadian misalignment can influence mood, although larger studies are needed to establish the long-term consequences.

Outside the laboratory, many people experience a mismatch known as [social jetlag](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27218855/). This occurs when people’s sleep and waking times differ substantially between working days and days off.

Artificial light can also affect our internal clocks. Bright light in the evening, including light from electronic screens, can suppress melatonin and delay our sleep time.

My [research on light sensitivity](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33049062/) has highlighted differences between individuals. Some people’s circadian rhythms are much more sensitive to evening light than others, meaning the same exposure may have different effects.

**Could Changing Meal Times Help?**

Light is the strongest environmental signal for the master clock, but eating also influences the timing of biological processes in other organs.

In a [2022 study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36095195/), my colleagues and I investigated whether changing meal times could reduce the effects of simulated night work on mood.

Nineteen healthy volunteers followed carefully controlled schedules designed to mimic night shifts. One group ate during both the day and night, while the other ate only during the daytime.

Among participants who ate during both periods, ratings of depression-like mood increased by 26.2% and anxiety-like mood by 16.1% compared with their baseline measurements.

We did not observe significant increases in either measure among those who ate only during the daytime.

These findings suggest that the timing of meals may influence how circadian disruption affects mood. However, the study involved a small group of healthy volunteers under laboratory conditions. Further research involving shift workers is needed to establish whether eating only during the daytime can help reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression.

**How to Support Your Body Clock**

Although we may not control our working hours or sleep schedules, some daily habits may help keep our internal clocks aligned.

1.   [Get morning daylight](https://theconversation.com/why-morning-blue-light-therapy-could-improve-sleep-and-daily-activity-in-older-adults-251576). Light is the most powerful environmental signal for the master clock. Spending time outdoors after waking can support alertness and help regulate the timing of sleep later. The amount of light needed varies between people.
2.   Reduce bright light before bed. Dimming household lights and limiting screen use in the evening/night-time may help the body prepare for sleep. The [NHS recommends](https://www.nhs.uk/every-mind-matters/mental-wellbeing-tips/how-to-fall-asleep-faster-and-sleep-better/) avoiding electronic screens for at least an hour before bedtime.
3.   Keep a regular sleep-wake schedule. Going to bed and waking up at reasonably consistent times can help reinforce circadian rhythms. A [systematic review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33054339/) associated regular sleep patterns with better health outcomes, including diabetes, heart diseases and depression.
4.   Consider food and exercise timing. Consistent and earlier food times may help support the body’s daily rhythms for physical health, although research is needed to establish the best eating schedules for mental health. Regular physical activity can also benefit sleep. A [review of studies](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30374942/) found that evening exercise generally did not interfere with sleep, although vigorous exercise ending very close to bedtime sometimes did.

**Protecting Sleep and Mental Health**

Research suggests that the timing of sleep and daily activities can influence mood, although more evidence is needed to establish whether changing these routines can help prevent or treat mental health conditions.

Maintaining consistent routines and getting enough sleep may support emotional wellbeing, but these habits cannot replace appropriate treatment. Anyone experiencing persistent sleep or mood problems should seek medical advice. Understanding how our internal clocks influence mood may eventually offer new ways to support mental health. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# Chimps Can Be Thieves, But They Hesitate to Rob Their Friends

And their friends were quicker to forgive them for their thievery

[DR](https://nautil.us/author/devinreese)

By [Devin Reese](https://nautil.us/author/devinreese)

9:00 AM CST on November 5, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/AdobeStock_921333115.jpeg?w=2880)

Humans obviously behave differently toward their friends than they do strangers. Case in point: We’re much more likely to loan money to a friend than a stranger. It appears that our closest relatives also differentiate between friends and strangers—especially when it comes to deciding who to steal treats from according to a [recent study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1090513826001273) published in the journal _Evolution and Human Behavior_.

Experimental psychologists watched 26 adult chimpanzees (_Pan troglodytes_) during 30-minute feeding times at the Ngamba Island Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Uganda to ascertain which ones were closely bonded via grooming each other, eating together, or otherwise making body contact or hanging out near each other. Next, chimps selected as study subjects were paired with either their closest “friend” or a not-very-close chimp. One chimp (the “victim”) was put in a room with access to three trays baited with large chunks of pineapple. Another chimp (the “thief”) watched the trays being loaded up, and, after the victim enjoyed one of the pineapple chunks, it was given the opportunity to steal the other pieces of fruit.

**Read more: “**[**What Became of the Chimps Who Revolutionized Our Understanding of Animal Behavior?**](https://nautil.us/what-became-of-the-chimps-who-revolutionized-our-understanding-of-animal-behavior-1282759)**”**

The researchers found that chimps stole more often (in 70 percent of trials) from non-friends than from friends (61 percent of trials).

[Subscribe to skip ads](https://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

“Ours is the first study to show that (chimpanzees are) able to hold back antisocial behavior with their friends,” explained lead study author Oded Ritov, a postdoc at the University of California, Berkeley, in a [press release](https://news.berkeley.edu/2026/09/30/chimps-plunder-less-pineapple-from-friends-and-expect-them-to-do-the-same/). “This suggests that there may be mutual expectations in chimps from both sides of the friendship, which makes it seem more like the complex friendships we see in humans.”

The apparent emotions of the chimps also differed depending on whether they were confronted with a friend on the other side of the pineapple or not. Stomping, screaming, and fist-pounding were taken as measures of negative emotions. The victims’ initial emotions during a theft were more intense if a friend did the plundering. Across trials, though, the anger against friends diminished, whereas it stayed high with non-friends.

The study authors hypothesized that, like humans, chimps have higher expectations of their friends, provoking a stronger reaction at first, but followed by forgiveness and a willingness to share. “We think that these expectations might be the basic building blocks of the larger-scale cooperation we see in humans,” added Ritov.

They may be the building blocks of our snarkiest behaviors too. ![Image 9](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# 7,500 Light-Years From Earth, A Cat’s Head Appears

A beautiful new NASA image of the Carina Nebula

[DN](https://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

By [David Nield](https://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

7:00 AM CST on November 5, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 3](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/cat_nebula_header.jpeg?w=2880)

Looking at the images [NASA just published](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/ghostly-cats-head-nebula-lurks-within-sight-of-nasas-hubble-webb/) from its Hubble and James Webb Space telescopes, you’d think part of the Carina Nebula was haunted. The vast cloud of gas and dust in these images resembles a cat sitting upright, with an eerily glowing eye.

[Video 7](blob:https://nautil.us/b6e93b94-8a6c-408b-b906-6f9c5b103c11)

[Video 8](https://nautil.us/7500-light-years-from-earth-a-cats-head-appears-1286346)

It’s called the Cat’s Head Nebula, a piece of the Carina Nebula that, while not newly discovered, has been newly zoomorphized and nicknamed. It’s around 7,500 light-years away from Earth, carved out over eons by intense ultraviolet radiation and winds from the massive stars that call this region of the universe home.

![Image 8](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/01-hubble.jpg?w=710)

A visible light image from the Hubble Telescope. _Credit: NASA, ESA, STScI; Processing: Joseph DePasquale / STScI_

That distinctive eye is thought to be a newly forged star, still largely cloaked in the dust that makes up the pillar shape that stretches below. Different densities of material are eroded at different rates, which gives us spectacular shots like these.

[Subscribe to skip ads](https://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

The Hubble Space Telescope image is the one capturing visible light, with the yellow ridges around the cat evidence of gas being ionized and lit up by ultraviolet radiation. Astronomers think photoevaporation might be happening here, which happens when gas is heated to such an extent it effectively boils off and disperses. You can also see oxygen lit up in blue, hydrogen glowing green, and sulfur burning red.

The two James Webb Space Telescope images chronicle the same scene in near-infrared and mid-infrared wavelengths, light that you wouldn’t see if you were peering out of a passing spaceship at the nebula. Near-infrared reveals some of the starlight partially hidden by dust, which is why the body of the cat looks more transparent. We get a better view of the background, though the thickest of the orange dust filaments are still visible.

![Image 9](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/02-webb-near.jpg?w=710)

A near-infrared view from the James Webb Space Telescope. _Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI; Processing: Joseph DePasquale / STScI_

The mid-infrared image is more about heat than light, and it’s the ghostliest of the lot—it really does look like a spectral feline keeping watch in space. The white outlines are created by the warmth of the dust and other carbon-based molecules that make up the Cat’s Head Nebula.

A mid-infrared image captured by the James Webb Space Telescope. _Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI; Processing: Joseph DePasquale / STScI_

As always with these shots, the colors are chosen at the image-processing stage; the telescopes are grabbing the light readings in black, white, and gray.

title: The Female Iron Age Queen Who Helped Bring Britain to its Knees
content:
In the early first century, a mighty king ruled the Atrebates tribe located in southern Britain: King Verica, son of Commius. As a client king of the Roman Empire, King Verica had a powerful ally in Emperor Claudius, who, in turn, enjoyed a foothold on the island. So when King Verica was exiled around 40 CE, it offered a pretext for Claudius to invade Britain (according to writings by the Roman historian Cassius Dio), sparking a campaign that would ultimately lead to the Roman conquest of Britain.

There’s just one problem with Dio’s story. King Verica wasn’t the son of Commius, she was the daughter of Commius—Verica was a female king. Or at least that’s the case archaeologist Miles Russell of Bournemouth University makes in a newly published book [_Caratacus: Great King of Britain_](https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/caratacus-9781350477902/).

**Read more: “**[**Mass Grave of Women and Children Shows Brutality of Iron Age Culture**](https://nautil.us/mass-grave-of-women-and-children-shows-brutality-of-iron-age-culture-1270456)**”**

“Verica is assumed to have been male because of the patriarchal mindset of 19th century, classical historians,” Russell explained in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1148686). “Verica wasn’t only critical to the special relationship between Britain and Rome in the early first century AD but was indisputably female.”

According to Russell, one of the most obvious clues is her name. Verica ends in an “a” like the names of other indisputably female figures at the time (including Boudica, who led a failed rebellion against conquering Roman forces later on).

The gender confusion centers, in part, around the word “rex” imprinted on coinage bearing Verica’s name which were found littered around Hampshire and Sussex where her tribe lived. Russell says Roman leaders tolerated and recognized female kings, and the term “rex” was a gender-neutral appellation. “The use of the Latin title rex on coins shows that Verica ruled with the full authorization of the emperor,” Russell explained.

And the coins contain more clues as well. The backs of the currency are stamped with the letters “COMF,” which historians initially read as an abbreviation of _Commios filius_, “son of Commios.” Russell points out they could just as easily be an abbreviation of _Commios filia_, “daughter of Commios.” Finally, the fronts of the coins depict a slender, bare-breasted woman—a pretty big sign Verica was female.

Of course, the revelation that Verica was a woman isn’t just a minor bit of historical trivia, it also provides important context for understanding of Emperor Claudius and the conquest of Britain. Claudius, a limping stutterer who suffered sickness early in life, was mocked by Cassius Dio and other writers as a weak leader who was easily swayed by wives. Verica being a woman obviously fits neatly with this reputation.

“The story of Claudius committing to something only because a woman told him to fits the trope of this emperor as being submissive and henpecked,” Russell said. “In effect, Dio was saying that the campaign was undertaken solely because of the whisperings of a barbarian femme fatale.”

It also casts the actions of both the female king and her powerful ally in a more strategic light. “The invasion was Claudius’ great triumph—it being the only chance he had to prove he was a successful military leader,” Russell said. “Verica provided the excuse for regime change and the emperor seized it.”

All that’s left is for someone to head over to Wikipedia to change Verica’s pronouns. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Archaeologists Unravel an 88-Year-Old Murder Mystery
content:
Around midday on January 10, 1938, renowned British archaeologist James Leslie Starkey called for a taxi to take him to the city of Jerusalem from Lasich, the ancient Canaanite and Israelite settlement he had been studying. Outside of Hebron, Starkey’s driver spotted five armed men with white headscarves covering their faces. They shot at the cab, and with the road too narrow to turn around, Starkey and the driver were trapped. The men beckoned the car to approach and then ordered both of them to exit. Once Starkey and the driver identified themselves, the band of brigands let the driver go. Starkey was later found dead.

British authorities investigating the murder focused on Issa al-Battat, a Palestinian rebel commander who had found himself on the wrong side of the ruling authority before. He commanded dozens of fighters, collected protection money from local villages, and had attacked a British police commander on a nearby road just a year earlier. Acting on a tip, British forces ambushed al-Battat in Hebron, killing him after a prolonged firefight.

**Read more: “[Was This Neanderthal Murdered?](https://nautil.us/was-this-neanderthal-murdered-1285819)”**

Starkey’s murder was ultimately chalked up to run-of-the-mill banditry by a gang of rebels—one of many amidst the diffuse violence that accompanied the 1936-1939 Arab Revolt. But now a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.5334/bha-749) in the _Bulletin of the History of Archaeology_ suggests his killing was a calculated assassination with a motive that complicates the story.

Archaeologists from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and the ​​Van Leer Jerusalem Institute reviewed British colonial records, Palestinian historical accounts, intelligence documents, and oral testimonies to paint a compelling picture of murder fueled by a desire for vengeance.

Starkey’s work, bankrolled by wealthy British patrons, focused on Lasich, the site of an Assyrian victory over the kingdom of Judah following a siege in 701 B.C. But his excavations led to conflicts with villagers of al-Qubayba currently living there—Starkey needed to dig beneath their farmland, and they needed their farmland to live. Negotiations dragged on for years before the al-Qubayba landowners finally agreed to sell. After receiving half their payment, the villagers tried to renege on the deal, leading British forces to forcibly expropriate their land.

The people of al-Qubayba were understandably angry at losing their livelihoods, something the researchers document in newly uncovered oral and written testimonies. One petition to the Director of Antiquities in Jerusalem by a “poor and weak” landowner complaining that he hadn’t received compensation years later was met with a dismissive letter instructing him to write to Starkey instead. Another report from a village historian “detailed the intense friction between local landowners and British excavators, framing the murder within the context of these agrarian grievances,” the researchers wrote.

To the researchers, this years-long grievance provides an undeniable motive for murder. According to the team, the site of the alleged assassination—miles from the village—was chosen to remove any suspicion. It seems to have worked. British authorities knew about the protracted conflict over land rights, but cleared any of the villagers of wrongdoing.

More importantly, the study offers a glimpse into a troubling history of colonial archaeology, providing “examples of how archaeological activity intersected with land disputes, social tensions, and anti-colonial sentiment in rural Palestine,” the researchers wrote.

Reliefs depicting the siege of Lasich were unearthed in the mid-19th century, but if you’d like to see them, you’ll have to travel to the British museum in London. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: What Happened When Neuroscientists Started a Mouse Fight Club
content:
The first rule of fight club is “you do not talk about fight club,” but the first rule of _mouse_ fight club seems to be “[publish](http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11217-9) your results in _Nature_.”

A team of Princeton neuroscientists recently set up a kind of sparring camp for lab mice to find out how watching a fight influenced their behavior. The team split the animals (all males) into three different groups: fighters, spectators, and novices. For the next eight days, each group engaged in a training regimen of sorts. The fighters sparred against a weaker opponent, the spectators watched two other mice fight, and the novices enjoyed a little play session with a mouse-shaped stuffed toy.

**Read more: “[What Darwin Overlooked About Fighting Female Animals](https://nautil.us/what-darwin-overlooked-about-fighting-female-animals-235829)”**

Then it was time to get in the octagon. All the experimental mice had to endure three four-minute rounds with an opponent who was no pushover. During the training and fights, god-like entities (okay, the neuroscientists) watched from above, filming their behavior.

Just like us, the team found that mice were enthralled by fights. “The observing mice don’t care so much when the fighting animals were just walking around and interacting,” study author Annegret Falkner explained in a [statement](https://pni.princeton.edu/news/2026/mice-watch-fights-come-away-battle-ready). “But we see them orient and attend once attacks start. Even if an attack starts and they’re not oriented, they’re more likely than chance to turn and watch what’s happening, so there’s something very salient and sticky about aggression that’s different from other behaviors.”

Watching the fights seemed to benefit the spectators when it was their turn in the ring. Both the spectators and the fighters were quicker on the attack and less likely to turn their backs than the novices. Interestingly, the time spent attacking was the same for all groups, suggesting that watching and fighting didn’t make those mice any more aggressive than the novices overall.

Of course, organizing a mouse fight club was the entire point of the experiment. The mice were genetically engineered with excitatory neurons that glowed green and inhibitory neurons that glowed red when they fired. To take a peek under the neural hood, the researchers inserted microthin fiber optic filaments into regions of their brains and watched the light show. When they viewed the fights, spectators’ inhibitory neurons fired like a fighter’s, but their excitatory neurons looked more like novice’s.

“They’re kind of midway between the truly experienced fighters and the naive animals,” Falkner said. “There’s something about experience that gets you all the way there, but observation gets you in a similar direction, but only about halfway.”

When spectators fought, however, both patterns resembled the fighter’s. Over the course of eight days, inhibitory cells surrounding aggression hubs eased up in both fighters and spectators. When the researchers tinkered with their neural activity to boost inhibition, these more experienced pugilists suddenly fought like novices again.

And according to the team, it might be possible to run the experiment in reverse. Now that they know what trained fighting neural activity looks like, they may be able to bestow those patterns onto a novice mouse, transforming it into a more skilled combatant.

“If you think about the photometry data as the musical staff of exactly what they just saw, we could replay all that activity back down to the circuit and give them the experience of watching, even though they never watched anything,” Falkner said. “If you replay back this sequence of activity and then you test them, do they behave as if they actually watched a fight?"

So what does that mean for us?

Obviously downloading years of krav maga into our brains isn’t on the immediate horizon, but the findings do suggest that witnessing violence may make us more prepared for it. “I have a hunch that probably some of these circuit changes are conserved in mice and humans," Falkner said.

Maybe watching kung-fu movies isn’t such a waste of time after all. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Myth of Mommy Brain
content:
“Science must begin with myths, and with the criticism of the myths,” reads the very first sentence of Susana Carmona’s new book [_A Mother’s Brain_](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262054782/a-mothers-brain/). The line is borrowed from _Conjectures and Refutations_, a foundational work in the philosophy of science published in 1963 by Karl Popper. Carmona picks up the gauntlet. She begins with the tenacious myth that mothers’ brains turn to mush the moment a baby begins to grow in their wombs, a cognitive fog that stretches into their final years. Then she spends the rest of the book complicating and reframing it.

For nearly two decades, Carmona, a neuroscientist, has been studying how motherhood remodels the female brain. In 2017, following publication of a landmark [study](https://www.nature.com/articles/nn.4458) in _Nature Neuroscience_, she established the Neuromaternal lab at the Instituto de Investigación Biomédica del Hospital Gregorio Marañón in Madrid.

**Read more:**[**“The Placenta Is More Powerful and Mysterious Than You Think”**](https://nautil.us/the-placenta-is-more-powerful-and-more-mysterious-than-you-think-1285683)

Motherhood, she has found, remaps the cortex, enhances plasticity, and triggers changes that not only cement the mother-baby bond and profoundly alter a mother’s sense of self, but can improve her well-being. A mother herself, Carmona weaves some of her own experiences into the narrative of her new book, giving her findings a first-person immediacy.

I spoke with Carmona recently about how motherhood is like adolescence, whether non-gestational mothers can experience some of the cognitive benefits of motherhood, and how little we understand about perinatal depression.

**Does motherhood hurt a woman’s memory?**

So far, our research suggests that memory deficits are restricted to the third trimester and the first years postpartum, but that over the long-term, there are improvements to cognitive function. We also learn a lot from the process of mothering: cognitive flexibility, tolerance for frustration, negotiation, working as a team, all skills that are very relevant not only for our personal life, but our professional life. A friend once told me she sees being a parent as doing a masters in humanity, because you see how everyone functions from scratch, what motivates them, what frustrates them, and how to deal with them.

**Why do the myths about mommy brain persist?**

Part of that comes because a high percentage of women report that their memory is not as it used to be. The problem is when you take that anecdote and turn it into a slogan, but you don’t get into the potential mechanism behind it. Until very recently, it was just something that we kept on repeating: “You have mommy brain.”

What our research group is trying to do is to evaluate that from a scientific perspective and understand the biological mechanisms, because gestation is metabolically demanding, and breastfeeding, too. A lack of sleep makes things worse. It doesn’t matter if you’re a mother or not. If you do not sleep, you’re going to have certain challenges cognitively speaking.

We also know that baby stimuli, especially within the postpartum period, really kidnaps the attention resources of the mother. Hearing your baby cry is not just another relevant auditory stimuli. It resonates throughout your whole body. It can make your breasts let down milk. That’s how powerful this physical resonance is.

But actually, when you look at the recent data, what they have found in middle-aged women, is that motherhood, either through biological mechanisms or more environmental ones, protects against brain aging. They have run these studies with the UK Biobank dataset, comparing mothers versus non-mothers. It doesn’t follow the same women over time, which would be the ideal design. It’s just mothers versus non-mothers. But they found fewer signs of brain aging in women who were mothers decades earlier. What we don’t know is whether there were differences at baseline.

**You write about this concept “matrescence,” a word I had never heard before. What does that word mean, and where does it come from?**

That word was coined for the first time by the medical anthropologist Dana Raphael in the 1970s. She used this term to refer to the fact of becoming a mother. But it never caught on. Later, Aurélie Athan, who’s a psychologist and psychiatrist, recovered this term and started talking about it from the psychological perspective and the psychiatric perspective.

What does it mean? It’s just a neologism that mixes motherhood with adolescence in order to highlight the parallelisms that take place between these two neuroendocrine transitions. During both periods, there is a redefinition of the self. There are also these hormonal fluctuations that not only change the body, but also change the brain. I think that the magic of this word is that it kind of overrides the narrative of momnesia.

The danger of giving priority to this term of momnesia is that when you believe something, you end up giving in to it. I know many women who just stop doing a master’s degree or other career aspirations because they believe that once you become a mother, you’re no longer going to have the same cognitive resources. You just have to take care of your kids because it’s the only thing you can do.

If you keep on believing this narrative of your brain without understanding the causes, it’s kind of dangerous. That’s what I like matrescence, because it highlights these other processes. In the end, we are the words we speak.

**You write that we need to do more research on what gets better for mothers cognitively. What kind of studies would you design to try to answer that question?**

Something that people keep on repeating, and I think it’s wonderful, is that parents are the second fastest learners, after their own children. I want to test that. We can make inferences by looking at the degree of neuroplasticity in the parental brain, but maybe what we should do is a longitudinal study and see whether they actually learn faster than other adults their age. I would love to know also whether their learning is only related to stimuli that have been linked to the baby somehow. For instance, do they learn a language more rapidly only when they are teaching that language to the baby? I think that could be an interesting question to explore. But I have many other questions more closely related to my field of research that I think are important to investigate first.

**What questions are those?**

The first publication about the brain changes in mothers was published almost a decade ago. But in scientific terms, that’s like yesterday morning. We found these profound changes, like nothing I’ve ever seen before, and I’ve seen many, many brain scans. Now, I want to know, for instance, how these brain changes relate to all the physiological changes that take place in the body of a woman. We have textbooks describing the cardiovascular changes, the immune changes, the metabolic changes. And now we have added the brain into the equation.

How do we mix all that together? How are these changes related? How are the immune changes affecting the brain changes? How do they communicate? And of course, one of our north stars is to try to use this data to prevent and predict perinatal mental health disorders.

So we have started to build the house with the roof: That’s a popular phrase in Spanish. We are trying to diagnose peripartum depression without understanding the profound changes that happen in neurotypical women during pregnancy. We need to better characterize these trajectories, not only in anatomy, but also in functional connectivity and cerebral blood flow, for instance. Once we know what normal looks like, we can try to identify potential deviations that might help us to predict and prevent perinatal mental health disorders. Those are my main questions right now, but I have many others.

**What are the existing explanations for perinatal and postpartum depression today?**

There are different mechanisms. It’s a multifactorial disease, like many other psychiatric disorders. We know there are imbalances in certain hormonal metabolites. We also know that birth experience plays an important role. We know that certain brain changes have been linked to these conditions. And on the other side of the spectrum, we know that social isolation, parental leave policies that are too short, economic stress, PTSD, or abuse during infancy are also linked to it. We’re trying to collect all this data. For some women, brain data and biological factors might play a bigger role, whereas for others, environmental aspects might play a more relevant role.

**Is there any evolutionary explanation?**

None of them really convince me. For instance, in rodents, when the mother perceives that conditions are poor—like temperature is bad or resources are lacking—they enter into a mood where they don’t take care of the babies or even attack them. You can imagine an evolutionary explanation for this, but I don’t really feel comfortable with it.

**How many of the changes in the brain and the body of the mother are tied to biological processes versus environmental ones? If you’re an adoptive mother or a stepmother, or you have a surrogate carry your babies because you cannot, do any of those processes still occur?**

I’m so happy you asked that question because I don’t want this research to be misunderstood. We have studies in which we compare the brains of women before and after they become gestational mothers. We also include non-gestational mothers in these studies, for example, when you have same-sex couples, to control for the biological effects and distinguish them from the environmental ones. We also include fathers. We use different control groups in order to disentangle the percentage of variance that exists in each group. And what I can tell you is that the data show very clearly that the brain changes that occur in gestational mothers are way more pronounced than in non-gestational mothers or in fathers, because the whole body changes.

Our breasts produce milk, our cardiovascular system pumps 50 percent more blood. We have dramatic hormonal changes in the brain. We have found that these changes facilitate or accelerate the onset of maternal caregiving, but they do not determine it and they are neither necessary nor sufficient.

What we have found is that there are also subtle changes in non-gestational mothers and fathers. They take place a little bit later and the magnitude is different. We don’t need a brain scan to make the claim that fathers and adoptive mothers and grandparents are fantastic caregivers.

So you can get into the caregiving effect, you can behave maternally through other routes. It doesn’t necessarily have to go through the gestational hormones. Just interacting with the baby, staying with the baby, caregivers learn to take care of the baby. And I love this sentence: We care because we love, but we also love because we care. It’s bi-directional. So in terms of brain changes, they are way more pronounced in gestational mothers. How these brain changes translate directly to caregiving, that’s an open question.

**I was wondering if you could talk a little bit about how microchimerism works, this idea that some DNA from a baby can remain in many of the mother’s organs long after birth. You point out in the book that there are a lot of unanswered questions, such as whether mothers have the DNA of miscarried babies in their tissue or whether it happens to all mothers.**

Most of these studies come from animal models, but in humans, what they have found is that women who had baby boys may carry XY cells in the brain. There are a lot of questions. For me, it sounded like science fiction. I performed a study on mice, and what I can tell you so far is that it’s not very common. It’s not that you find these baby cells in every single mother, but they exist, and sometimes it happens. It’s possible that it tends to happen when there has been certain danger to the mother, and these cells that are left behind are there because they migrated in order to help repair tissue damage, for instance, from a C-section.

Another thing that is important is that they usually talk about cells containing the DNA of the baby, but it might be that just exosomes or little vesicles with the DNA of the baby inside stay behind. It’s not something that I’ve been doing much research on but I have many questions: How do they cross the blood-brain barrier to get into the brain tissue? Are these holdovers stem cells that keep on regenerating? But what the literature is showing is that cells with the DNA of the baby migrate into the mother in a widespread way, not only on the brain, but also the liver, the breast tissue, the C-section tissue.

There are many pieces that I’m still trying to connect. But I know that a number of researchers now are trying to study whether this process contributes something positive for the mother or triggers autoimmune disorders, which are more common in women.

**A mother’s brain is very activated by her child, as you note, and she can find it almost difficult to resist attending to the child’s crying. What is it about the specific mother-child bond that allows her to respond in this instinctive way to her own baby?**

There are some studies that say that from the very beginning, a mother can recognize the smell of her baby, but these findings are kind of controversial. Some studies replicate the effect, but others do not. But mothers do learn to identify their own baby’s cries. And it’s not a normal learning process. It’s a learning process in which the stimuli is so relevant that you’re highly motivated to learn about it, because it’s very distressing. It’s not normal auditory stimuli. It’s something that resonates in your body.

That doesn’t mean that it’s always a pleasure to interact with the baby, just that you are very motivated to learn about the baby, because the baby’s discomfort can be very distressing and the baby’s pleasure, very rewarding. The mother is not going to give up, like, “Oh, I don’t understand this baby.” Her wonderful motivation is going to keep her insistent despite the mistakes. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)
